book: Going Deeper with New Testament Greek
notes: Every card carries a mnemonic hook, a one-line definition, a 'spot it' test you can actually run on a text, and real examples.
Greek is given in the text with the key word marked by * asterisks *, so the app can highlight it without any markup engine.
confusions[] are the pairs that actually get missed on a quiz. They are drilled separately from the cards.
extraQuiz[] are hand-written 'Spot it' items; the rest are generated from each card's examples.

sets.name: Nominative
sets.subtitle: The naming case — the case that puts the crown on someone
sets.bigIdea: The nominative NAMES. Whatever wears it is being named, identified or hailed — never acted upon.
sets.masterMnemonic: Go to the SPA, then say AAAH.
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: SPA = the three major uses (Subject, Predicate nominative, Apposition). AAAH = the four other uses (Address, Appellation, Absolute, Hanging). Seven uses, two words, one silly picture: you sit down in the spa and go aaah.

sets.name: Accusative
sets.subtitle: The case of limitation — the case that puts a fence around the verb
sets.bigIdea: The accusative LIMITS. It says how far the verb's action reaches: onto whom, how far, in what way, with respect to what.
sets.masterMnemonic: One object with four twists, then the MMR shot.
sets.masterMnemonicWhy: Substantival = the direct object plus four twists on it — Echo, Two, Sub, Alias. Adverbial = the MMR shot: Measure, Manner, Respect — How far? How? How so?

groups.name: The idea
groups.expand: The nominative crowns; the accusative fences.

groups.name: Substantival — one object, four twists
groups.expand: Direct object, then: Cognate (Echo), Double (Two), Subject of infinitive (Sub), Apposition (Alias)

cards.name: Subject
cards.oneLine: The nominative that performs the verb — the one the sentence is about.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The nominative is the naming case, and the crown sits on whoever the verb is about. If a verb has exactly one nominative near it, that nominative is wearing the crown.
cards.spotIt: Ask the verb "who or what?" — and check that the answer is nominative, not accusative.

examples.note: Ἰωάννης is nominative and does the witnessing — the plainest kind of subject there is.
One verb, one nominative, no complications.

cards.name: Predicate Nominative
cards.oneLine: Two nominatives joined by a copulative ("to be") verb; the predicate nominative asserts something about the subject.
cards.mnemonic: The subject is the small circle; the predicate is the big one.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The copula looks like an equals sign, but it is not a two-way street. "The Word was God" puts the Word inside God — not God inside the Word. Draw the small circle inside the big one and the whole doctrine of John 1:1 sits in one picture.
cards.spotIt: Look for a to-be verb — εἰμί, γίνομαι, ὑπάρχω — with a nominative on both sides of it.

examples.note: ὁ λόγος has the article, so it is the subject; θεός is the predicate nominative.
ὁ θεός is articular and so is the subject; ἀγάπη is what is asserted about him.
αὐτός is a pronoun, so it takes the subject slot outright — see the pecking order.

cards.watchOut: Apposition looks similar but has no to-be verb. Verb ⇒ predicate nominative; comma only ⇒ apposition.

cards.name: The Pecking Order
cards.oneLine: When two nominatives sit around one to-be verb, this is the order that decides which one is the subject.
cards.mnemonic: PAP — ask Papa who is in charge.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Pronoun, then Article, then Proper name. Papa answers in that order every time: a pronoun wins outright; failing that, the one with the article is the subject; failing that, the proper name.
cards.spotIt: Work down the list and stop at the first hit. 1. Is either one a pronoun? 2. Does either one have the article? 3. Is either one a proper name?

examples.note: No pronoun, so rung two decides: ὁ λόγος has the article and is therefore the subject. θεός is the predicate nominative — not "a god". In Greek a word can be perfectly definite with no article at all.
Rung one: αὐτός is a pronoun, so it is the subject even though ἡ εἰρήνη carries the article.

cards.watchOut: Anarthrous ≠ indefinite. "No article" is not an argument for "a god"; it is what a predicate nominative before the verb normally looks like.

cards.name: Apposition
cards.oneLine: Two nominatives side by side where the second renames or elaborates the first — with no verb between them.
cards.mnemonic: No verb, just a name tag.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Apposition is a sticker slapped on the first noun: "Andrew — HELLO MY NAME IS the brother of Simon Peter." Diagram it with an equals sign under the first word; there is no verb to hang anything from.
cards.spotIt: Two nominatives, a comma's worth of pause between them, and no copula anywhere.

examples.note: ἀδελφός is the appositive. Nothing is being asserted — he is simply being identified.
δοῦλος apposits Παῦλος.
Name tag. Compare "Ivan is the student" — that one is a predicate nominative, because there is a verb making a claim.

cards.watchOut: The whole difference from a predicate nominative is the to-be verb. Comma = label. "Is" = claim.

cards.name: Nominative of Address
cards.oneLine: A nominative doing a vocative's job — calling out to someone directly.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The word is being hailed, not described. It is logically the subject of the imperative that follows, but grammatically it is not the subject of anything.
cards.spotIt: Try putting a comma and an exclamation mark after it. "Husbands! — love your wives." If that works, it is address, not subject.

examples.english: Have mercy on us, *Son of David*
examples.note: Son of David is not doing the having-mercy in a subject sense — he is being called out to. The form is nominative; the function is vocative.
Not a statement about husbands. A summons to them.

cards.watchOut: A subject is talked ABOUT. An address is talked TO. Same case, opposite direction.

cards.name: Nominative of Appellation
cards.oneLine: A title used as a personal name, kept in the nominative even where the syntax was expecting another case.
cards.mnemonic: The title is on the name badge — and badges don't decline.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Once "Teacher" is what people actually call him, it stops behaving like a noun in a sentence and starts behaving like the name printed on a badge. (Second hook if you have any Spanish: appellation ≈ apellido, "surname".)
cards.spotIt: The word is a title, it is being quoted as what someone is called, and it is in the nominative when the surrounding grammar wanted an accusative.

examples.greek: ὑμεῖς φωνεῖτέ με *ὁ διδάσκαλος* καὶ *ὁ κύριος*
examples.note: φωνεῖτέ με wants an accusative complement, but the titles stay nominative — they are functioning as the name itself.

cards.watchOut: This is the simplest of the four 'other' uses. If a nominative is plainly a title-as-name, stop looking for anything cleverer.

cards.name: Nominative Absolute
cards.oneLine: A nominative with no grammatical connection to any sentence — usually a heading, a title or a greeting.
cards.mnemonicWhy: A headline floats above the page attached to nothing. No verb, no clause, no rope — it is just announced.
cards.spotIt: Introductory material — a book title, a salutation, a list — with no verb anywhere to attach it to.

examples.english: *The beginning* of the gospel of Jesus Christ
examples.note: ἀρχή is nominative and stands entirely alone; every word hanging off it is genitive.

examples.english: *Grace, mercy, peace* from God the Father
examples.note: All nominative, all introductory, all grammatically independent.

cards.watchOut: Absolute has NO rope. If a pronoun later in the sentence picks the word back up, it is hanging, not absolute.

cards.name: Hanging Nominative
cards.oneLine: Grammatically independent like the absolute, but logically the subject — picked up later by a pronoun.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The pronoun downstream is the rope. Cut the pronoun and the word drops — which is exactly the difference from an absolute, which was never tied to anything.
cards.spotIt: Find the stray nominative, then look ahead: is there a pronoun in the next clause standing in its place?

examples.greek: τὸ δὲ καλὸν *σπέρμα*, οὗτοί εἰσιν οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς βασιλείας
examples.english: and the good *seed* — these are the sons of the kingdom
examples.note: σπέρμα is grammatically loose, but οὗτοι ("these") is doing its job in the main clause. That pronoun is the rope.

cards.watchOut: Absolute = no connection at all. Hanging = a logical connection with no grammatical one.

cards.name: The Case of Limitation
cards.oneLine: The accusative limits or specifies the action of the verb.
cards.mnemonic: The nominative crowns; the accusative fences.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Every accusative use is a fence post: it marks how far the verb's action goes — onto whom (direct object), how far (measure), in what way (manner), with respect to what (respect).
cards.spotIt: Two families to sort into: does it behave like a noun (substantival) or like an adverb (adverbial)?

examples.ref: The whole chapter in one line
examples.english: One object with four twists — Echo, Two, Sub, Alias — then the MMR shot: Measure, Manner, Respect.
examples.note: Substantival first, adverbial second.

cards.name: Direct Object
cards.oneLine: The thing the verb's action lands on — far and away the most common accusative.
cards.mnemonic: The verb throws; the object catches.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Everything else in the substantival family is a twist on this one throw, so fix the plain case first.

examples.note: Ivan catches the hitting.

cards.name: Cognate Accusative
cards.oneLine: A direct object that shares the verb's lexical root, or its concept.
cards.mnemonic: Echo — the object echoes the verb.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Twist one of four. Say the verb and hear it come back: sing a song, fight a fight, shepherd a flock.
cards.spotIt: Say the verb and the object out loud. If it sounds redundant in English, it is cognate.

examples.note: Same root twice — the tightest kind of echo.
Not the same root, but the same concept — a conceptual echo still counts.
The textbook case.

cards.watchOut: It is still a direct object. Cognate names the flavour, not a different slot.

cards.name: Double Accusative
cards.oneLine: Two accusatives in one clause — either person + thing, or object + complement.
cards.mnemonic: Two — "ask someone something" vs "call someone something".
cards.mnemonicWhy: Twist two of four. Both types have two accusatives; the two English frames keep them apart. You ASK a person FOR a thing. You CALL an object A NAME.
cards.spotIt: Try to slip "as" or "to be" between the two accusatives. If it fits, it is object + complement. If it does not, it is personal + impersonal.

examples.note: him (personal) + bread (impersonal). You cannot say "asks him AS bread".

examples.english: to give his *life* as a *ransom* for many
examples.note: life is the direct object; λύτρον is the complement. "As" slips right in — object + complement.

cards.name: Accusative Subject of the Infinitive
cards.oneLine: An infinitive takes its subject in the accusative, where a finite verb would take a nominative.
cards.mnemonic: Sub — finite verbs pay in nominative, infinitives pay in accusative.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Twist three of four. The odd one out: this accusative is doing the action, not receiving it. Infinitives simply pay their staff in a different currency.
cards.spotIt: Find the infinitive, then find the accusative that is performing it rather than catching it.

examples.note: "Him" is doing the going. In Greek that word is accusative, and it is the infinitive's subject.

cards.watchOut: The only accusative that translates as the doer. If "the one doing it" fits, you are here.

cards.name: Accusative of Apposition
cards.oneLine: The same move as nominative apposition, in accusative dress: a second accusative renaming the first.
cards.mnemonic: Alias — the name tag, now on the object.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Twist four of four. If you have the nominative name tag, you already have this one; only the case changed.
cards.spotIt: Two accusatives, no verb between them, and the second answers "which one, exactly?"

examples.english: they chose Stephen, *a man* full of faith
examples.note: Στέφανον is the direct object; ἄνδρα apposits it.
Ἰσραήλ apposits λαόν.

cards.watchOut: Do not confuse with a double accusative. Apposition renames; a complement predicates something of the object.

cards.name: Accusative of Measure
cards.oneLine: Extent or degree — how far, how long, how much.
cards.mnemonicWhy: The three adverbial accusatives come as one MMR jab: Measure, Manner, Respect. Measure is the one with a tape measure on it.
cards.spotIt: Ask "how far / how long?" and see whether the accusative answers.

examples.note: μικρόν measures the distance, not the object of any verb.

cards.name: Accusative of Manner
cards.oneLine: How the action is carried out.
cards.mnemonicWhy: Manner turns the noun into an adverb: δωρεάν stops being "a gift" and becomes "gift-wise", i.e. freely.
cards.spotIt: Ask "how?" — and check that an -ly adverb is the natural English.

examples.note: δωρεάν = freely, as a gift. It describes the manner of the justifying.

cards.name: Accusative of Respect
cards.oneLine: Limits the scope of the verb — supply "with reference to" or "concerning" when you translate.
cards.mnemonic: MMR, shot three: How so? — slot in "as to".
cards.mnemonicWhy: The fence at its narrowest. The verb happened, but only in one respect, and this accusative names that respect.
cards.spotIt: Say the clause with "with respect to" in front of the accusative. If that rescues the sense, you have found it.

examples.english: they were pierced *with respect to the heart*
examples.note: Not a physical piercing of an organ — an inner wound. "With respect to" is what keeps it from sounding surgical.

cards.watchOut: Easy to mistake for a direct object. If "with respect to" makes the sentence better rather than worse, it is respect.

confusions.question: Predicate nominative or apposition?
confusions.answer: Verb ⇒ predicate nominative (a claim). No verb, just a comma ⇒ apposition (a label).
confusions.example: "Ivan is the student" (claim) vs "Ivan, the student, came to class" (label).

confusions.question: Absolute or hanging?
confusions.test: Does a pronoun later in the sentence pick the word back up?
confusions.answer: No rope at all ⇒ absolute. Hangs by a pronoun ⇒ hanging.
confusions.example: Mark 1:1 "The beginning of the gospel…" (headline) vs Matt. 13:38 "the good seed — THESE are the sons…" (rope).

confusions.question: Address or subject?
confusions.test: Is the person being talked about, or talked to?
confusions.answer: Talked about ⇒ subject. Talked to ⇒ address, however nominative the form looks.
confusions.example: "Husbands love their wives" (subject) vs "Husbands, love your wives" (address).

confusions.question: Two nominatives round one verb — which is the subject?
confusions.test: Run PAP: pronoun, then article, then proper name.
confusions.answer: First hit wins. In John 1:1c ὁ λόγος has the article, so it is the subject and θεός is the predicate nominative — definite, not "a god".

confusions.question: Cognate or plain direct object?
confusions.test: Does the object echo the verb — same root, or same concept?
confusions.answer: Echo ⇒ cognate. No echo ⇒ just a direct object. Either way it is still the object.
confusions.example: "Fight the good fight" (echo) vs "I hit Ivan" (no echo).

confusions.question: Two accusatives — which arrangement?
confusions.test: Can you slip "as" or "to be" between them?
confusions.answer: "As" fits ⇒ object + complement. "As" does not fit and one is a person ⇒ personal + impersonal. No verb and the second merely renames the first ⇒ apposition.
confusions.example: "gave his life AS a ransom" (complement) vs "asks him for bread" (person + thing) vs "chose Stephen, a man full of faith" (apposition).

confusions.question: Accusative of respect or direct object?
confusions.test: Put "with respect to" in front of it.
confusions.answer: Sense improves ⇒ respect. Sense gets worse ⇒ direct object.
confusions.example: Acts 2:37 "pierced WITH RESPECT TO the heart" — better. "I hit WITH RESPECT TO Ivan" — worse.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Grace, mercy, peace from God our Father" (1 Tim. 1:2) — all nominative, no verb, opening a letter.
extraQuiz.why: Introductory material with no grammatical tie to anything. A headline, not a rope.

extraQuiz.prompt: "You call me Teacher and Lord" (John 13:13) — the titles are nominative where you expected accusative.
extraQuiz.why: A title functioning as the name people use. Badges don't decline.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Son of David, have mercy on us" (Matt. 9:27).
extraQuiz.why: He is being hailed, not described. Nominative form, vocative job.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus" (Rom. 1:1) — two nominatives, no verb.
extraQuiz.why: δοῦλος renames Παῦλος. No copula, so no claim is being made — it is a label.
A copula with a nominative each side. αὐτός is a pronoun, so it takes the subject slot; ἡ εἰρήνη is what is asserted.

extraQuiz.prompt: "The good seed — these are the sons of the kingdom" (Matt. 13:38).
extraQuiz.why: σπέρμα is grammatically loose but οὗτοι picks it up. Hanging by a pronoun.
The object echoes the verb — same root, even.

extraQuiz.prompt: "He gave his life as a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45).
extraQuiz.why: Two accusatives, and "as" slips between them: object + complement.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They were cut to the heart" (Acts 2:37) — an inner wound, not a surgical one.
extraQuiz.why: Supply "with respect to" and the sense improves.

extraQuiz.prompt: "Going a little farther, he fell on the ground" (Mark 14:35).
extraQuiz.why: μικρόν answers "how far?" — MMR shot one.

extraQuiz.prompt: "They chose Stephen, a man full of faith" (Acts 6:5).
extraQuiz.why: ἄνδρα renames the direct object. Alias.

extraQuiz.prompt: An infinitive's subject — the one performing the infinitive's action.
extraQuiz.why: Finite verbs take nominative subjects; infinitives take accusative ones.

extraQuiz.prompt: "and the Word was God" (John 1:1c) — which use is θεός?
extraQuiz.why: ὁ λόγος has the article and wins the pecking order, so θεός is the predicate nominative. Anarthrous, and still definite.
